newsitem.title: UK: Britain's B.A.T posts lower profits, holds dividend steady.
newsitem.headline: Britain's B.A.T posts lower profits, holds dividend steady.

text.p: B.A.T Industries Plc reported a 5 percent drop in half-year profits Wednesday and said it would hold its dividend payments steady due to uncertainty about the proposed tobacco settlement in the United States.

B.A.T, whose Brown & Williamson subsidiary is the third-largest cigarette maker in the United States, said pretax profits in the six months ended June 30 fell to 1.25 billion ($2.04 billion) from 1.31 billion pounds ($2.14 billion) -- mainly due to a 61 million pound ($99.5 million) impact from the strength of the pound sterling.

The company also said in a surprise announcement that it would hold its dividend payments steady due to the potential cost of the tobacco settlement. Analysts had expected the company to declare a modest increase in the dividends it pays twice a year.
"It's a case of short-term pain for long-term gain," spokesman Michael Prideaux said. "We think it would have been misleading given the short-term uncertainty to have carried on as usual."

At the same time, however, B.A.T tried to assure investors that the proposed landmark settlement of legal claims against the tobacco industry in the United States was unlikely to affect other countries.

"Shareholders may well be concerned about whether the proposed resolution will also affect other countries. We do not consider that it will," Chairman Lord Cairns in a statement accompanying the group's half-year results.

American tobacco companies -- including Brown & Williamson, whose brands include Kent, Lucky Strike and Kool -- agreed with state attorneys general in June to settle most legal claims against them in return for payments totalling $368.5 billion over 25 years.
If the settlement terms are approved by Congress, B.A.T would be obliged to pay $1.7 billion up-front. The second payment into the fund comes due one year after enactment.

B.A.T said its profits from tobacco rose 6 percent to 800 million pounds ($1.3 billion) -- excluding the 22 million ($35.9 million) cost of closing a cigarette factory in Germany and 21 million ($34.3 million) for a legal settlement in Mississippi. The group's total cigarette volumes were flat.

The company reported a strong increase in tobacco sales in Latin America, supporting its rationale for the acquisition, announced July 22, of Cigarerra La Moderna, the leading cigarette maker in Mexico, for $1.7 billion.

The group's Lucky Strike brand showed strong sales in Germany and Spain while total profits in Europe jumped 41 percent to 86 million pounds ($140.3 million), reflecting higher cigarette prices, especially in Germany.
